query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the cooling rate during solidification to refine the eutectic lamellar spacing in high-entropy alloys will simultaneously boost tensile strength and ductility by optimizing the balance between the hard and soft phase distributions.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a moderate lamellar spacing with alternating soft (fcc) and hard (B2) phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid solidification process (i.e., increase the cooling rate during casting) to produce a finer, more uniform lamellar microstructure.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed at room temperature on eutectic HEAs for structural applications, comparing specimens made with conventional cooling versus enhanced cooling rates.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced lamellar spacing that increases the dispersion of fine fcc/B2 phases.
generation.mechanism: The finer lamellar structure provides more barriers to dislocation motion, elevating strength, while maintaining continuous soft phase paths that facilitate dislocation transmission and plastic deformation, thereby increasing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens produced via rapid solidification will show a higher tensile (or fracture) strength relative to conventionally cast alloys while also exhibiting improved elongation (ductility).
generation.baseline: Conventional cast eutectic high-entropy alloys with coarser lamellar spacing.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the cooling rate is optimized; excessively high cooling may introduce high residual stresses or non-equilibrium phases, which could negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and may depend on the alloy composition and processing details; potential adverse effects due to residual stresses also need to be assessed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same eutectic HEA: one group using conventional casting methods and another group using a process with a significantly increased cooling rate (rapid solidification). Characterize their microstructures (e.g., lamellar spacing via SEM) and perform room temperature tensile tests to quantify strength and ductility.
measurements: Lamellar spacing via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid solidification specimens do not exhibit both a refined lamellar microstructure and a concomitant simultaneous increase in tensile strength and elongation compared to the conventionally cast specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
